sentences.text:
The Honourable Smt. Justice K. Sujana
 Criminal Petition No.10763 of 2023
Order:

This Criminal Petition is filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 by the petitioners, who are arrayed as accused Nos. 3 and 4 to quash the orders passed in Crl.M.P.No.130 of 2023 in C.C.548 of 2023 on the file of the learned VI Additional Junior Civil Judge-cum-VI Additional Metropolitan Magistrate at L.B.Nagar for the offences punishable under Sections 465,
468, 471, 420, 506 read with 34 IPC.

2. Brief facts of the case are that on 25.12.2021, respondent No.2 gave a complaint to the Police wherein it is mentioned that on 06.03.1992, respondent No.2 along with accused No.1 purchased a plot bearing No.49 in Sy.No.140, 142/1 admeasuring 371 sq.yards situated at Karmanghat Village from one Sri. Vangara Narayana Reddy vide document No.2861/1992.

It is stated that accused Nos.1 and 2 forged the signature of respondent No.2 and sold the said plot to accused No.3 on 21.06.1999 at SRO, Champapet vide document No.3597/1999 by suppressing the fact that accused No.2 is the joint owner of the said plot along with accused No.1.
Thereafter, when respondent No.2 questioned accused Nos.1 and 2 about selling the said plot by using forged documents to accused No.3, they have threatened him with dire consequences.

3. Based on the complaint, the police registered a case vide Crime No.1046 of 2021, dated 25.12.2021 for the offences under Sections 465, 468, 471, 420, 506 read with 34 IPC against accused Nos. 1 to 4.
Since the involvement of accused Nos.3 and 4 was not established, their names were deleted from charge sheet.

Against the said deletion, respondent No.2 filed Crl.M.P.No.130 of 2023 under Section 202 of Cr.P.C to take cognizance of the offence against accused Nos. 3 and 4, on the file of learned Metropolitan Magistrate and the trial Court allowed the same by taking cognizance for the offences under Sections 465, 468, 471, 420, 506 read with 34 of IPC.

4. Heard Sri T.Srujan Kumar Reddy, learned counsel for the petitioners, Sri S.Ganesh, learned Assistant Public Prosecutor for respondent No.1-State and Sri A.Ananthasen Reddy, learned counsel for respondent No.2 5.

Learned counsel for the petitioners firstly contended that accused No.3 along with accused No.4 purchased the said plot and from the date of purchase, they are in continuous possession of the said property.

He secondly contended that respondent No.2 after lapse of 22 years filed complaint in the year 2021 and though the police deleted the names of the accused Nos. 3 and 4 from the charge sheet after thorough investigation, the trial Court allowed the Crl.M.P.No.130 of 2023 by taking cognizance against the petitioners.

He lastly contended that respondent No.2 also filed O.S.No.155 of 2023 on the file of Principal Senior Civil Judge, Ranga Reddy District at L.B.Nagar, in which,
accused No.3 filed the written statement and therefore, he prayed the Court to allow the criminal P. Rama Devi vs The State Of Telangana on 12 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135104451/
1 petition by quashing the proceedings against the petitioners/accused Nos.3 & 4.
6.

sentences.text: On the other hand, learned counsel for respondent No.2 contended that the petitioners purchased the said plot knowingly that the said plot is a joint property of accused No.1 and respondent No.2.

Therefore, he prayed the Court to dismiss the criminal petition.
7.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the judgment of Mohammed Ibrahim and others Vs. State of Bihar and Another 1, dated 04.09.2009 at paragraph Nos.14 to 17 observed hereunder:
14.

entities.text: Mohammed Ibrahim and others Vs. State of Bihar and Another 1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
An analysis of section 464 of Penal Code shows that it divides false documents into three categories:
1) The first is where a person dishonestly or fraudulently makes or executes a document with the intention of causing it to be believed that such document was made or executed by some other person, or by the authority of some other person, by whom or by whose authority he knows it was not made or executed.

2) The second is where a person dishonestly or fraudulently, by cancellation or otherwise, alters a document in any material part, without lawful authority, after it has been made or executed by either himself or any other person.

3) The third is where a person dishonestly or fraudulently causes any person to sign,
execute or alter a document knowing that such person could not by reason of (a)
unsoundness of mind; or (b) intoxication; or (c) deception practised upon him, know the contents of the document or the nature of the alteration.

(2009) 8 SCC 751 In short, a person is said to have made a `false document', if (i) he made or executed a document claiming to be someone else or authorised by someone else; or (ii) he altered or tampered a document;
or (iii) he obtained a document by practicing deception, or from a person not in control of his senses.
15. The sale deeds executed by first appellant, clearly and obviously do not fall under the second and third categories of `false documents'.

It therefore remains to be seen whether the claim of the complainant that the execution of sale deeds by the first accused, who was in no way connected with the land, amounted to committing forgery of the documents with the intention of taking possession of complainant's land (and that accused 2 to 5 as the purchaser, witness, scribe and stamp vendor colluded with first accused in execution and registration of the said sale deeds) would bring the case under the first category.

P. Rama Devi vs The State Of Telangana on 12 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135104451/
2 16.

entities.text: P. Rama Devi vs The State Of Telangana on 12 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: There is a fundamental difference between a person executing a sale deed claiming that the property conveyed is his property, and a person executing a sale deed by impersonating the owner or falsely claiming to be authorised or empowered by the owner, to execute the deed on owner's behalf.
When a person executes a document conveying a property describing it as his, there are two possibilities.
The first is that he bonafide believes that the property actually belongs to him.
The second is that he may be dishonestly or fraudulently claiming it to be his even though he knows that it is not his property.
But to fall under first category of `false documents', it is not sufficient that a document has been made or executed dishonestly or fraudulently.

There is a further requirement that it should have been made with the intention of causing it to be believed that such document was made or executed by, or by the authority of a person, by whom or by whose authority he knows that it was not made or executed.
17. When a document is executed by a person claiming a property which is not his, he is not claiming that he is someone else nor is he claiming that he is authorised by someone else.

Therefore,
execution of such document (purporting to convey some property of which he is not the owner) is not execution of a false document as defined under section 464 of the Code.
If what is executed is not a false document, there is no forgery.
If there is no forgery, then neither section 467 nor section 471 of the Code are attracted.
8. Having regard to the rival submissions made by both the parties, the offences alleged against the petitioners are under Sections 465, 468, 471, 420, 506 read with 34 of IPC.
The allegations against these petitioners in the complaint are that they have conspired with accused Nos.1 and 2 and knowingly purchased the plot from accused Nos.1 and 2.
To constitute offence under Section 463 IPC averments must show that petitioners created false document to cause loss to the original owner.
The averments show that Accused Nos. 1 and 2 sold the property to these petitioners stating that they are the absolute owners.
Mere purchasing the property from Accused Nos. 1 and 2 does not constitute any of the offences alleged by the prosecution.
Merely alleging that Accused Nos.3 and 4 are not bonafide purchasers is not sufficient to constitute alleged offences.
As such, in order to attract the offence alleged against the petitioners, the averments must show that accused Nos. 3 and 4 forged the documents of the said plot to cause loss to the complainant.

In the present case, the allegation is only knowingly these petitioners purchased the property, whereas, there is no forgery as defined under Section 463 of IPC.
9.

Therefore, in view of the above discussion and principles laid down in the aforesaid judgment,
since there are no averments in the prosecution case to prove that these petitioners created false documents and cheated respondent No.2, the proceedings against the petitioners are liable to be quashed.

10. Accordingly, the Criminal Petition is allowed and the proceedings against the petitioners/
accused Nos. 3 and 4 in Crl.M.P.No.130 of 2023 in C.C.No.548 of 2023 on the file of VI Additional Junior Civil Judge-cum-VI Additional Metropolitan Magistrate at L.B.Nagar are hereby quashed.
